platforms.title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Isn't a Typing Injury
platforms.meta_description: Numbness that wakes you at 3am rarely comes from a keyboard. What the NHS and NIAMS actually list as causes, and the signs that mean stop waiting.
platforms.body_html:
You wake at three in the morning with a hand that feels dead, hang it over the side of the bed and shake it for thirty seconds, and the feeling comes back. It happens again the following week, then most weeks. Somewhere in the search that follows, someone will tell you this is what a keyboard does to people. Before you buy the gel wrist rest, it is worth knowing that the official cause lists for carpal tunnel syndrome do not mention keyboards at all — and that the studies which looked hardest for the link came back with nothing.

What the Official Cause Lists Actually Say

The carpal tunnel is a narrow passage at the base of the palm, floored by wrist bones and roofed by a stiff band of ligament. One nerve, the median nerve, shares that space with nine tendons that bend the fingers. The National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) describes the median nerve as supplying feeling to the thumb, index and middle finger and part of the ring finger — but not the little finger — and as controlling some of the small muscles at the base of the thumb. When tissue inside that tunnel swells, the nerve is the structure with nowhere to move.

NIAMS is unusually blunt about why the swelling happens: “Researchers do not know the causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.” The contributing factors it lists are trauma or injury to the wrist, mechanical problems in the wrist joint, repeated use of vibrating machinery, problems with the pituitary or thyroid gland, rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases, diabetes and other metabolic disorders, fluid retention during pregnancy or menopause, adult age, and being female. The NHS list runs in parallel: being overweight, being pregnant, work or hobbies that involve repeatedly bending the wrist or gripping hard — such as using vibrating tools — arthritis or diabetes, having a parent or sibling with the condition, and a previously injured wrist.

Read both lists again and notice what is absent from each.

The Keyboard Question, Answered With Numbers

This has been studied properly, more than once. A 2015 meta-analysis by Shiri and Falah-Hassani in the Journal of the Neurological Sciences pooled six studies of nearly 5,000 people comparing computer workers with the general population or other occupational groups, and found a pooled odds ratio of 0.72 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.90) — computer workers had fewer cases, not more. A 2014 review in the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine found meta-odds ratios of 1.67 for computer use, 1.11 for keyboarding and 1.94 for mouse use, with every confidence interval crossing 1, and concluded it was not possible to show an association.

The largest test is the most recent. A 2022 systematic review in Health Science Reports pooled 17 prospective cohort studies covering more than a million workers and graded the evidence. High computer-use exposure was associated with a decreased rate of work-related carpal tunnel syndrome (hazard ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.64). What did raise the rate, with high-certainty evidence, was repetition (HR 1.87) and force intensity (HR 1.84) — gripping and squeezing hard, over and over. None of this means office work is protective; people who type for a living differ from people who bone poultry in many ways besides their hands. It does mean the keyboard is the wrong thing to worry about.

Skip the Wrist Rest — Here Is What the Trials Support

The interventions with the most evidence behind them are unglamorous, and the honest summary includes their limits.

  • A night splint — the NHS advises wearing one while you sleep to hold the wrist straight, and warns it may take up to six weeks before it starts to feel better. A 2023 Cochrane review of 29 trials in 1,937 adults found splinting may give little or no symptom benefit versus no active treatment in the short term, though night-time splinting may produce a higher rate of overall improvement. It is cheap and its harms are minor, which is why it stays first in line.
  • Cutting back the exposures that are actually on the list — the NHS names using vibrating tools for work or playing an instrument, not typing. Repeated hard gripping is the pattern to interrupt.
  • Treating what is treatable underneath — thyroid disease, diabetes and weight all appear on both cause lists. If you have not had bloods done, that is a reasonable thing to raise.
  • Time, in pregnancy — the NHS notes carpal tunnel syndrome sometimes resolves by itself within a few months, particularly when it started during pregnancy.

Beyond that, a steroid injection or surgery may be offered. A 2024 Cochrane review of 14 trials found surgery probably produces a higher rate of clinical improvement than splinting in the long term (risk ratio 2.10, 95% CI 1.04 to 4.24), while the difference in symptom and function scores was probably not clinically important. Those are genuine trade-offs, and they are a conversation to have with a clinician rather than a decision to reach on your own. Do not stop or change any prescribed medicine because your hand feels better.

The Signs That Mean Stop Waiting

This is the part the habit-and-posture articles leave out. NIAMS describes what chronic or untreated cases look like: the fingers feel numb all the time rather than in bursts, and the muscles at the base of the thumb become so weak that it is difficult or impossible to grasp small objects — buttons, zips, coins. That thumb pad shrinking is muscle loss following nerve damage, and it does not reliably come back.

Germany’s Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care puts the timing plainly in its patient guidance: when the nerve is not yet badly damaged and there is no persistent numbness or muscle loss, symptoms usually improve within a few weeks of surgery — which is exactly why it can make sense not to postpone the decision too long. The NHS advice is to see a GP if symptoms are getting worse or are not going away, or if treating it yourself is not working.

So before the shopping: over the past month, has the numbness stayed in bursts you can shake off, or has it started sitting there through the day — and can you still feel the coin you are picking up? This article is general health information, not a diagnosis. Which of those two answers you gave is the thing to bring to the appointment.
